prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The monocular depth map shows a top-down outdoor scene where the camera wearer looks down at their own bright white torso and arms (0.1 to 0.6 m away) standing above a cluster of mid-grey boulders on the left (1.0 to 1.8 m below the head) and darker grass and mulch on the right (1.5 to 2.0 m down). A grey plastic bin sits to the lower left within the wearer's arm's reach (0.5 to 1.2 m away), and a second person stands to the right at roughly 1.2 to 1.8 m from the wearer and 1.0 to 1.5 m from the rocks, with only their lower legs, right hand, and a long-handled tool entering the right edge of the frame while their upper body and head remain out of view (preventing determination of whether they look at the wearer, though their feet face left toward the wearer and rocks). Across the five frames, the camera wearer steps backward and turns slightly clockwise away from the boulders—which recede from 0.6 m within arm's reach in frame 1 to 1.5 m in frame 5—lifts and tilts the bin with both hands in frame 4 before setting it down on the lower left in frame 5, and reaches their right arm forward (~0.6 m) to grasp the tool handle held within the second person's arm's reach on the upper right. The depth map makes the 3D relief and step-down heights of the stacked boulders, the hollow interior depth of the tilted bin, and the overhanging bush foliage on the upper left of frames 4 and 5 much clearer than in the flat RGB image. However, it is unreliable inside the dark opening of the bin in frame 1 (which appears artificially deep) and along the thin tool shaft in frames 3 and 4, which blends into the dark ground plane.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates foreground body parts and objects against an unlabelled black background where the boulders, mulch, and lawn at 1.0 to 2.0 m below the camera are completely omitted. In frame 1, it separates the camera wearer's left arm, torso, and right arm (0.1 to 0.6 m away, extending forward and downward from the bottom edge) into three distinct 'person' masks while missing the adjacent bin to the lower left; in frames 2 and 3, the wearer's torso, legs, and right arm merge into a single central 'person' mask (0.1 to 1.2 m) as the wearer steps back from the boulders and turns right. In frames 3 and 4, the second person's legs entering from the right edge (1.2 to 1.8 m from the wearer, facing left toward the wearer with their upper body occluded outside the frame) are segmented at the middle right, and in frame 5 the second person's hand holding the tool on the upper right (~0.8 m from the wearer, within both people's arm's reach) and lower torso on the far right are segmented separately from the wearer's reaching right arm. Compared to RGB alone, the masks sharply delineate the boundary between the wearer's hands and the held bin in frame 4 as well as the exact silhouette of the wearer's baggy shirt and arms against the textured ground. However, the map is highly unreliable in its class labels and completeness: it misclassifies the held grey bin in frame 4 (at 0.5 to 0.9 m) as a 'cell phone' and the second person's legs in frames 3 and 4 as a 'cow' and 'horse', while completely failing to segment the bin in frames 1–3 and 5, the tool shaft, and the boulders.
descriptions.pose: The pose map renders only 2D magenta hand skeletons on a completely black background, detecting no yellow body skeletons in any of the five frames because the camera wearer's head-mounted viewpoint looks steeply downward at their own torso (0.1 to 1.5 m below) and truncates the second person on the right to only their legs and hand (1.2 to 1.8 m away). In frame 1, a single open hand skeleton is detected at the upper right where the wearer's right hand presses flat against a boulder within arm's reach (~0.6 m away), while the wearer's left arm on the upper left is partly out of view and unmapped. In frame 2, as the wearer releases the rock and retreats slightly, the map tracks both of the wearer's hands—the left hand gripping the bin rim on the lower left (~0.5 m away) and the right hand hovering above the rocks and pants (~0.6 m away, separated from the left hand by ~0.5 m). Frame 3 is entirely blank despite the wearer's right hand and the second person's feet being visible in RGB, whereas frame 4 captures both of the wearer's hands grasping opposite sides of the tilted bin's rim (~0.4 to 0.6 m in front of the torso and ~0.3 m apart) before frame 5 again shows no detections despite both people's hands holding the tool shaft on the upper right (~0.6 to 0.8 m away). Where present, the pose map reveals exact finger articulation, palm orientation, and grip geometry on the rock and bin rim that are visually subtle against similar skin and surface tones in RGB, but it is unreliable whenever hands are partially self-occluded, motion-blurred, or near the frame edges in frames 1, 3, and 5, and provides zero information about full-body posture or gaze direction.
